  `multiple-pins`. Without a pin, the latest commit on the default branch is
  used. **Pins are strings**: `@piton/config` types them as strings, so
  `tag: 1.0` stays `"1.0"`. Other pin diagnostics are `dangling-pin` and
  `unknown-pin`.
- **Picking packages.** A repository can offer several packages. You get all
  of them unless you list the ones you want with `packages:` under the URL:
  `packages: [ui-kit]`.
- **Project and package dependencies are separate.** The project's apply only
  to the project, and each package declares its own.
- **No nested dependencies.** When two packages need the same package at
  different versions, **the one with the newest commit wins** and a warning is
  shown.
- **Installation.** Each package goes into `tethers/<name>`, next to
  `piton.config.pi`, with the files from its `root`. A repository offering
  `ui-kit` and `my-package` gives `tethers/ui-kit` and `tethers/my-package`.
  Tethering removes every trace of git. A repository that offers no packages
  is installed whole, under the name its URL implies.
- **Importing.** An installed package is a location placeholder:
  `from my-package import X`, `use my-package`, `use my-package/MyAnchor`.
  Normal path resolution applies below it. A missing package is a compiler
  error.
- **Lock file.** `.piton/tether.lock`, next to `piton.config.pi`, keeps each
  tethered package's URL, commit and a hash of its files. `tether` and
  `update` write it, and it is committed with the project.
- **Conflicts.** Before tether, update or any other operation on an installed
  package, the tooling compares its files with the lock file and goes ahead
  only if nothing changed. If the files were edited, it says so and asks the
  user to untether (or `piton update --force` to discard the edits).

The commands:

- `piton tether` on its own installs everything in `dependencies`. Given a
  source URL, it adds it to `dependencies` in `piton.config.pi` and installs
  it. `--as <name>` installs under another name.
- `piton update [packages...] [--force] [--diff]` reinstalls from
  `dependencies`, all packages when none are named. `--force` replaces a
  package even if it was edited, discarding the edits with a warning;
  `--diff` prints a coloured unified diff of every file each update changed.
- `piton untether <package>` moves the package from `tethers/` to
  `<root>/untethered/` and rewrites the imports that named it, making it the
  project's own source. `--as <name>` renames it; `--no-rewrite` only moves
  it.
- `piton remove <package>` deletes an installed package and removes it from
  `dependencies`. It refuses if the files were edited or if anything still
  imports the package.

## 13. CLI reference

Every command prints what it produced first, then a one-line outcome (✓ or
✗), and its problems last: diagnostics, errors and warnings with their help
and notes, then the error and warning count. On a terminal the output is
coloured and paths are marked `+`/`-`; piped or with `NO_COLOR`, it is plain
text and stdout carries the bare results.

| Command | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `piton check [paths...]` | Validates syntax, imports, references, types, inheritance, composition, exports and circular dependencies, reporting errors and warnings. Writes nothing. Exits 0 when there are no errors and 1 otherwise. Paths are optional files, directories or globs; the default is the project (or every `.pi` file under the working directory when there's no `piton.config.pi`). |
| `piton build [config] [--dry-run]` | Builds the project configured by `piton.config.pi` (or the given config). Writes renderer output to `<output>/<path under root>.<ext>` (defaults: `./dist`, JSON), so `spec/components/Button.pi` becomes `dist/components/Button.json`: the entry file plus every file holding something the entry's exports reference. A registered framework's output replaces it unless the config sets `output` or `renderer`, which asks for both. Records every file in `.piton/manifest.json`. The whole plan is validated before anything is written. `--dry-run` reports without writing. |
| `piton compile <path> [--renderer json\|yaml\|markdown] [--write] [--dependencies]` | Compiles one file to stdout (JSON by default): one key per export. `--write` writes `<file>.<ext>` next to each input and is required for globs. `--dependencies` wraps the result as `{"value": "<compiled output as a string>", "dependencies": [absolute source paths]}` so build tools know what to watch; bundled package files are left out. |
| `piton format [path] [--check]` | Applies canonical formatting (4-space indents, constraint spacing, sorted and wrapped imports, no `.pi` in import paths, a space after `//`). `--check` reports without writing. `piton format -` reads source from stdin and writes the formatted text to stdout. It **only splits overflowing lines and never rejoins a paragraph**, so rewrap edited prose by hand, and don't reflow `key: value` blocks as prose. |
| `piton reach [targets...] [--no-unreachable] [--no-paths]` | Starting from files, globs or anchor names (the entry by default), follows outgoing imports, references, inheritance and composition, direct and transitive. Reports what is reachable with its depth and the path taken, and what is unreachable. The flags hide the last two. Use it to find dead spec. Grouped by source, with a summary. No diagnostics; always exits 0. |
| `piton slice <target> [--adapter <target>]` | Prints the part of the spec one thing depends on, as one Markdown document for an agent's prompt. The target is `file.pi#Anchor`, `file.pi#Anchor.property`, `file.pi#variable`, or a bare name looked up across the project (an error when more than one file declares it). Follows, transitively: what an anchor extends, every base that also declares a property, anchors named by type constraints, what a value read (`${Other.x}`, variables), and what it references or embeds. Imports alone bring nothing in. A whole anchor needs all its properties and bases; slicing a property leaves out the anchor's other properties; a reference to a property needs only that property. It also includes the **chain** from the project's entry down to the target (`Specification.Tooling`, `Tooling.cli`, `Cli.commands`): the shortest path the build takes, each link only that one property and not followed further. An export of the entry, a variable, and a file the build doesn't reach have no chain. Order: the target, then its dependencies nearest first (source order breaks ties), then the chain outermost first, so the same source prints the same bytes. Each declaration appears once, headed by its name as written (`SaveButton.color`), with its file, what it extends, its type and what it reads. References and embeds are written as names; cycles are followed until they come back around. Every path it prints is relative to the directory it runs in, and it finds the project by looking upward for `piton.config.pi`. `--adapter claude-code` (any Belay target the project builds) cites the compiled output instead: each location and every reference links to where `piton build` writes it (an embedded anchor to the section that embeds it), and no `.pi` file is ever cited; an abstract base or an anchor that is only read has no document of its own and is described without one. With `--adapter` the target itself must be something the build writes out. Markdown links the author wrote pass through unchanged. Exits 1 on errors. |
| `piton init [directory] [--template <group/name>] [--adapter <id>...] [--list]` | Starts a new project from a template compiled into the compiler (no network needed). Templates come in groups: `piton/minimal` (plain Piton to JSON), `piton/library` (a package others can tether), `belay/application` (a shape instruction placed in `src/`, a skill, an agent and a command) and `belay/minimal` (the Belay config and one skill). Without a directory it first asks for the project's name and creates that directory (an empty answer, or no terminal, uses the working one). Then it asks for a group and a template (`--template belay` asks only for the template), and for a Belay template, which adapters to build for: a checklist of Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode with the template's default (Claude Code) checked, or `--adapter`, repeated or comma-separated. The chosen adapters replace the config's import and `adapters` list, and a template's `.adapters/<id>/` files (like OpenCode's `opencode.json`) are written only for the adapters chosen. Templates are the `group/name` directories in the compiler repo's `create-templates/`, each with a one-line `.template` description that is not written out; adding one is adding a directory, and every template must check cleanly, be formatted, and build. `--list` describes the groups and templates and does nothing else. With no terminal, a full template name is required. It never overwrites a file: if any it would write exists, it names each and writes none, and cancelling a question writes nothing. Prints each written path on stdout, then a summary and the next commands on stderr. Exits 1 on errors. |
| `piton loc [paths...]` | Counts total, code, comment and blank lines per file, with a summary. Defaults to the project. No diagnostics; always exits 0. |
| `piton lsp` | Runs the language server over stdio (section 14). |
| `piton agent [claude] [--print-fluency] [args...]` | Launches the agent with a short project primer plus this fluency prompt (the project's `FLUENCY_PROMPT.md`, or the copy built into the compiler), passed to `claude` as `--append-system-prompt`. Extra arguments go to the agent. `--print-fluency` prints the prompt and does nothing else. |
| `piton tether [source] [--as name]` | See section 12. |
| `piton update [packages...] [--force] [--diff]` | See section 12. |
| `piton untether <package> [--as name] [--no-rewrite]` | See section 12. |
| `piton remove <package>` | See section 12. |

Each CLI command in the spec is a `cli-command` anchor
(`spec/scope/tooling/cli/index.pi`) with `commandName`, `positionalArguments`
and `namedArguments`.

## 14. Language server, editors, and JavaScript

`piton lsp` provides, from the spec's feature list:

- Diagnostics (not for missing optional properties), completion, hover (type,
  source, documentation, inheritance chain, export status and compiled
  interpretation), go-to-definition, find-references, and rename across the
  whole specbase.
- Auto-import, import organization, and code actions: import a missing
  symbol, create an unresolved anchor, add an export, qualify an ambiguous
  reference, resolve a simple inheritance conflict.
- Document and workspace symbols, semantic highlighting, inlay hints
  (resolved types, inherited origins, composition sources), formatting,
  folding and selection ranges.
- Inheritance, composition (`+`, `++`), override and conflict resolution;
  reference resolution; validation and type information for expressions in
  `{}`, `${}`, `#{}` and `@{}`; export validation; module resolution; cycle
  detection (circular imports are fine and not reported).
- Related-symbol navigation, a hierarchy view, resolved-value and provenance
  inspection, compiled-output preview, source-to-output mapping, unused and
  redundant definition detection, and documentation integration.
- Incremental analysis and workspace indexing.
- Diagnostics cover Belay semantics as well as Piton. Import organization
  flags unused, duplicate, invalid and overly broad imports. Cycle detection
  also catches an anchor that ends up extending itself, and shows the cycle.

There is no signature help.

Completion rules: never suggest things that don't exist; offer nothing on an
empty value (`property: `), because prose probably follows; offer nothing
after a `.` inside a string.

Editing rules every editor must follow, through the LSP or the editor
extension:

- Enter after a colon that opens a dictionary or anchor property starts a new
  line indented one level deeper.
- Enter on a blank line inside a dictionary or anchor starts a new line one
  level shallower.
- Format-on-save is optional. It adds the space after `//` and touches nothing
  else that is commented.

Supported editors and their highlighters (spec): VS Code (TextMate plus LSP);
Emacs, Helix and Zed (tree-sitter plus LSP); Neovim and Vim (vim syntax);
JetBrains (`jetbrains`); Sublime (sublime-syntax); Kate (KSyntaxHighlighting).
Every editor gets full LSP support. The integrations live under `editors/`.

**Consuming Piton from JavaScript.** `packages/vite-plugin-piton` imports
`.pi` files as modules, with HMR, dependency tracking (through
`piton compile --dependencies`) and virtual modules. Each export in the Piton
file is a named export, and the default export is the whole file, the same as
`piton compile` gives:

```ts
import { SaveButton } from '../spec/app.pi';
import spec from '../spec/app.pi';

const button = SaveButton;
const cancel = spec.CancelButton;
```

It has a configurable default renderer (`renderer: 'json' | 'yaml' |
'markdown'`), and the renderers can also be imported as functions
(`vite-plugin-piton/renderers`) and used inline. `packages/astro-piton` is an
Astro integration that wraps the Vite plugin.

## 15. Working on a specbase

1. **Orient.** Open `piton.config.pi` to find `root`, `entry`, `output`, the
   frameworks, the adapters, `codeRoot` and `shapeRoot`. Read the entry file,
   usually `spec/index.pi`, because its exports are the compilation roots.
   Follow the `index.pi` files down through the modules. In this repository,
   `spec/index.pi` exports `Specification` (FoundingThesis, Language, Tooling,
   Belay, PackageManagement) plus the skills and command in `spec/agent/`.
2. **Read compiled reference for overview, and source for truth.**
   `<referenceRoot>/**/*.md` is easy to browse, and its links are lazy, so
   follow them only when relevant.
3. **Edit the `.pi` source**, following the conventions around it:
   - one exported anchor per file, named after the file;
   - `index.pi` files that re-export with `from ./X export *`;
   - abstract anchors exported with a keyword, and shared abstracts in a
     `lib/` folder;
   - lowerCamelCase property names;
   - SCREAMING_CASE for exported constant lists;
   - prose in string blocks, and structure in keys and lists;
   - `@{X}` to link related documents;
   - examples inside fences wrapped in a `\\\` escape block.
4. **Keep imports honest.** Use `use` for keywords and `from ... import` for
   names; a file often needs both. A new file only compiles if the entry
   reaches it, so export it through an index or reference it.
5. **Validate.**
   - Run `piton check`.
   - `piton check` does **not** compile the examples inside escape blocks
     (they are literal text). When you edit spec examples, extract each ` ```piton ` block,
     run `piton compile` on it, and compare with any ` ```json ` block that
     follows. Remember that compile output has only exported names.
   - Run `piton build`, then look at the diff of the generated files.
   - Run `piton reach` to confirm new anchors are reached.
   - Run `piton format --check`.
6. **Never hand-edit generated files.** That includes `CLAUDE.md` and
   `AGENTS.md` under `codeRoot`, everything under `.claude/`, `.codex/`,
   `.agents/`, `.opencode/` and the build output directory that is listed in
   `.piton/manifest.json`, and the files in `.piton/` themselves.
7. **Keep implementation and spec in agreement.** The implementation is judged
   against the spec. When they disagree, report it instead of quietly bending
   the spec to fit. Trust `piton compile` for how things behave today, and
   flag the gap.

## 16. Where the compiler differs from the spec

Checked with `piton compile` and `piton build`:

- The CLI has a few things the spec doesn't name: `build --dry-run`,
  `tether --as`, agent argument passthrough, the `reach` flags, and
  `format` with no path or `-`.

- **Paragraph breaks.** The spec says a blank line in a string block starts a
  new paragraph. The compiler joins the paragraphs with a single `\n`, which
  Markdown output renders as one paragraph with a soft line break.

Known limitations, where the spec is silent and the compiler's choice may
surprise you:

- A `/`-rooted import inside an installed package resolves against the
  consuming project's root, not the package's. Use relative imports inside a
  package.
- A required property from an abstract is not satisfied by a value inherited
  from a concrete base (`needs Thing extends Base`, where `Base` supplies it):
  the keyword's anchor comes last, and its value-less declaration wins. Give
  the value on the anchor itself.
- `piton check` with no paths checks what the entry reaches, so a file that
  nothing imports is not checked. Name it: `piton check path/to/file.pi`.
- **Prose directly in an anchor body is silently dropped.** `anchor A:` with
  only a line of text under it (no key) compiles to an empty anchor, with no
  diagnostic. Always put prose under a key, such as `description:`.
- Mixed-type equality is simply unequal: `{1 == "1"}` is `false`, not an
  error. The spec says `==` works on every type but doesn't spell this out.
- Which constructs each adapter requires a `description` for (section 11.2)
  is hardcoded in `crates/piton-belay/src/adapter.rs`, not declared in the
  adapter `.pi` files.

A Planning should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A Planning should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, integration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [Theme](../../ui/theme/index.md#theme): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Pitch

A plain, quick list of the work still to do, as Linear keeps issues: stories written ahead of time, each saying how it will be sent, Code, Chain, Spec, Ask, or Freeform, gathered into the next sprint and sent to the agent in order, all at once.

## Description

Planning opens in a tab of its own in the body, "Planning", with a checklist icon, as a file opens, as the [Body](../application/Body.md#body) says, from the ribbon's Planning tab or the palette's "Planning". It is a kanban board, filling the body beneath the tab bar, as the [Body](../application/Body.md#body) places it, from the tab bar down to the chat input and from the body's left edge to its right. Its sections sit side by side as columns, in the order work moves, left to right: "Backlog", "Next sprint", "Current sprint", and "Done", then "Findings", the last, as research says. Each column is headed by its name and count, with its actions, as the layout says, and holds its stories as cards, one beneath another. Every column is always there, whatever it holds; one with nothing in it shows its empty state, as the states say.

## Stories

A story is one piece of work, written as it will be sent: a title, a prompt, and how it will be sent. Each is a story card in its column, as the parts say, quiet and dense, as Linear keeps an issue, showing all a story shows: a drag grip at its top left; its title beside it, the card's one primary thing, in the body's text colour, wrapping onto a second line and cut off with an ellipsis only after that; and beneath the title, a single muted property row of small

### Items

a small mode picker, a pill reading its mode, "Code", "Chain",

"Spec", "Ask", or "Freeform", in that mode's colour, as the [PromptModes](../prompt-mode/modes/index.md#prompt-modes) colours it; its step count and a small icon for anything attached, when it has them; and, once it has been sent, its status, as a task's is shown, at the row's right. Hovering a card shows a menu button at its top right. A story has no Send of its own, as the sprint says.
A column is too narrow to open a story in place, so clicking a card never expands it beneath itself or moves the cards below it: it opens the story in the side panel, docked at the board's right, as the layout places it and the parts draw a panel, headed by the story's title. The panel holds all an open story holds: its title, editable in place; its prompt, in a [GrowingTextInput](../../ui/components/growing-text-input/index.md#growing-text-input) with the chat input's highlighting, completions, and slicing, as the [ChatInput](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input) has, and its attachments beneath; its parameters, its mode, model, effort, and Slice, as the chat input shows them; its steps, with Add step, as its steps say; and its Spec citations, as the spec grounding says. Every change is saved as it is made. While its story is open, its card stays highlighted, its line in the theme's accent, so which story the panel shows is always plain. Only one story is open at a time: clicking another card opens that one in the panel instead. Escape, the panel's close button, or clicking the open story's card again closes it, and its card's highlight with it.

## Creating

Creating a story is quick, as adding a card is in Trello and adding an issue is in Linear: a story is added in the list it belongs in, right where it will sit. The Backlog and Next sprint each end with an "Add story" line at their foot, beneath their last card, or beneath their empty state when they have none. Clicking it opens a composer in its place: a blank story card, drawn as the parts draw one, whose title is a text box, focused, in the mode last picked for a story, with nothing else to fill in. Typing a title and pressing Enter adds the story to that list, where the composer was, and opens another composer beneath it, so a list can be written down without the mouse. Enter with the title empty adds nothing. Escape discards the composer, and whatever was typed in it, and the "Add story" line comes back; clicking away while its title is empty discards it too, and clicking away with a title typed adds the story, as Enter does, but opens no other composer. A story added this way is not opened in the side panel; its card is there to be clicked, as the stories say, once more than its title is wanted.
Hovering the Backlog's or Next sprint's heading shows a labelled "+ Add" button in it, as the layout places it, which opens the composer at the top of that list, above its first card, so a story can go first without being dragged there; Enter adds it there and opens the next composer beneath it, so stories written one after another keep the order they were written in. Ctrl+N (Cmd+N on macOS) while Planning has focus opens the composer at the foot of the list that has focus, the Backlog or Next sprint, as the keyboard says, and at the foot of Next sprint when neither has it. Only one composer is open at a time: opening another discards an empty one and adds one with a title, as clicking away does. Current sprint, Done, and Findings have no "Add story" line, no "+ Add", and no composer, and Ctrl+N never adds a story to them.
A story goes into the list it was added to, then: the Backlog or Next sprint, whichever composer it was written in. A duplicate goes into its original's list, just beneath it, and a story added from an Ask answer's card with "Add to sprint" goes into Next sprint, at its end. An accepted proposal for a new story, from drafting, research, or an Ask answer's proposal card, still goes into the Backlog, at its end, as the proposal cards say, and reaches a sprint only once it is moved to Next sprint. A story can always be moved between the two afterwards, as the sprint says. Adding a story never starts a sprint by itself, except where Start automatically starts one when a story is added to an empty Next sprint, as auto start says; a story added to the Backlog never starts one. A title with no prompt sends its title as its prompt.
A story can also be prompted into existence: "Draft stories", a button beside the Backlog's heading, opens a small box to say what is wanted, in a sentence or a paragraph, and asks the harness, in a run of its own with no session, with the planning prompt of the [BakedSystemPrompts](../harness-integration/baked-prompts/index.md#baked-system-prompts), to break it into stories, each with a title, a prompt, and the mode that fits it. They come back as proposals, as the drafting and proposals say, each to be accepted, edited, or rejected, and none reaches the plan until it is accepted. An Ask answer's prompt cards also offer "Add to sprint", which adds the card's prompt as a story in its mode to Next sprint.

## Sprint

Stories move between the Backlog and Next sprint by dragging, as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, a card dragged by its grip from one column into a gap in the other as within either, the gap opened in the column the pointer is over, as motion says; an empty one takes a drop at its top. Dragged near the board's left or right edge, the board scrolls sideways, and near a column's top or bottom, that column scrolls, as dragging says. Only the Backlog and Next sprint take drops: Current sprint and Done open no gap, a story dropped on them stays where it was, and their cards can't be picked up, nor can a finding. Stories move too from a card's menu, "Move to next sprint" or "Move to backlog". Their order within Next sprint is the order they will be sent. A card's menu also has "Duplicate" and "Delete".
"Send sprint", a primary button at the right of Next sprint's heading, enabled while it holds a story, sends every story in it, in order, as though each had been written in the chat input on its mode's tab and sent, one after another, as the [PromptSending](../prompt-mode/sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says: each task queues in its lane behind the one before it, in the order of the sprint, and each question runs at once. The stories go into the queue as one block, so nothing sent later comes between them, and the queue's auto-send carries them on as ever, as the [QueueList](../prompt-mode/queue-list/index.md#queue-list) says.
Each story starts a conversation of its own, as though New conversation had been pressed just before it, and so does each later step of a story's chain: a story never carries on the conversation of the story before it, nor of anything its lane ran before the sprint. New conversation, pressed before the sprint was sent, is left for the next prompt written in the chat input.
A story can't be sent on its own. The only way a story reaches work is through the sprint: a story in the Backlog waits until it is moved into Next sprint and the sprint is sent, and a story in Next sprint goes when the sprint does. Nothing in Planning, its cards, their menus, the open story, the keyboard, the palette, or the ribbon, sends a single story, and nothing elsewhere sends a story by any other route: a story can't be dragged or copied into the chat input or the queue to be sent from there, and its menu has no "Send" or "Edit in chat input". The chat input's own prompts are not stories and are sent as ever; once a prompt is a story, the sprint is its only way to work. To send one story at once, it is the only story in Next sprint when Send sprint is pressed. A story that failed or was cancelled is sent again the same way, with the next sprint.
Sending the sprint moves its stories into the "Current sprint" column, to the right of Next sprint, so Next sprint is empty again and stories added meanwhile go there, to be the sprint after. Current sprint and Done are columns of the board whatever they hold, never appearing, disappearing, or collapsing; while no sprint is under way Current sprint is empty and shows its empty state, as Done does before anything is done. A story in Current sprint keeps its place, its card showing its task's status as it queues, runs, and ends, and clicking it opens its task in the Tasks tab; it can't be moved or edited there. Once every story of Current sprint has ended, its column's heading offers "Close sprint", which moves the stories that are done into the Done column, their cards muted, and those that failed, were cancelled, or stopped to the start of Next sprint, in their order, to be sent again. While a sprint is current, Send sprint is disabled, its tooltip saying a sprint is already under way.
Send sprint only ever moves into Current sprint the stories it actually sent. A story with nothing to send, its title and its prompt both empty, is skipped: it stays in Next sprint, where it was, and Send sprint's result says, muted, how many it skipped and why, as "1 empty story left in Next sprint". A sprint where every story is empty sends nothing and makes no Current sprint.
Once a sprint is done, it can always be closed. Every story of Current sprint counts as ended once its task has ended, done, failed, cancelled, or stopped, or once its task can no longer be found, as when its record was deleted, it was never recorded, or the application quit before it was. A story whose task is missing is never shown as Queued, or as anything still to come: its card reads "Task missing", muted, in the theme's warning colour, its tooltip saying its task can't be found, and it counts as ended and not Done. A story still waiting in its lane's queue, or held for review, as the paused section says, is still to come and hasn't ended. So Close sprint shows as soon as no story of Current sprint is building, compiling, running, paused, queued, or held, and never waits on a task that can't arrive.
Close sprint treats a story whose task is missing as it treats one that failed or was cancelled: it goes back to the start of Next sprint, with the others sent again, in their order, never into Done. Closing saves the sections, Done, Next sprint, the Backlog, and the emptied Current sprint, to `order.json` straight away, as the [ProjectData](../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, and Current sprint's state is worked out afresh from the stories' tasks whenever the plan is read, so a sprint that finished, or whose tasks went missing, before a reload or a restart can still be closed after it, as before.

## Motion

Dragging a card on the board feels as it does in Trello, and the board opens the gap, as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) lets its user do, in place of the accent line alone. Only the board's cards move this way; steps in an open story, and every other list, are dragged as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, with its line.
A card picked up by its grip lifts off the board as a full-size copy of itself, the same width and height, drawn as the parts draw a story card, tilted a few degrees, about 3, on the theme's overlay surface with its edge border and the soft shadow the [Theme](../../ui/theme/index.md#theme)'s elevation gives floating surfaces, the one shadow on the board. It follows the pointer, held where it was grabbed, and never takes the mouse. The card's own place in its column becomes the gap it left, empty, the card's height, so the column doesn't jump as it lifts.
Where the card would land, the cards slide apart to open a placeholder the dragged card's height, 8 pixels from the cards either side, as the cards are spaced: a box the card's size on the theme's well surface, with its corners rounded 6 pixels as a card's are, and no border, so it reads as an empty slot. The gap is chosen as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) chooses it, among the cards of the column the pointer is over, and only one is open at a time: as the pointer moves into another gap, or another column, the gap it left closes as the new one opens, and the gap the card came from closes once the pointer leaves its column, opening again if it comes back. A column that takes no drops opens no gap, and its cards never move while a card is dragged over it.
Nothing waits on motion while the user is waiting on it. The gap the card would drop into is updated at once, the moment the pointer crosses the middle of a card, exactly as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, and a drop always goes where the gap was chosen, even while the cards are still sliding toward it; only the sliding of the cards around it is animated, quickly, as below.
Dropped over an open gap, the copy settles into it: it straightens, its shadow fades, and it moves from where it was released into the placeholder, which it then is, the story saved in its new place at the moment of the drop, as every change to the plan is. Dropped anywhere else, or where it began, it settles back into the gap it came from the same way, and nothing changes. Escape while dragging cancels it, settling the card back where it was.
A card moved any other way animates to its new place, in Linear's

### Style

a quick motion of about 150 milliseconds, eased out, sliding

from where it was to where it now is, the cards it passes or leaves sliding to close and open the room it takes, never fading or bouncing. That covers every move the sprint describes: "Move to next sprint" and "Move to backlog" from a card's menu, Alt+Up, Alt+Down, Alt+Left, and Alt+Right, Ctrl+Enter, Send sprint moving its stories into Current sprint, and Close sprint moving them into Done and back to the start of Next sprint. A card added, as by a composer or Duplicate, slides the cards below it down to make room, and a card deleted slides them up to close it, in the same motion. The board scrolls sideways, and a column up or down, to keep a moved card that has focus in view, as the keyboard says. Focus goes with the card at once, not when its motion ends, and the plan is saved at once.
The side panel slides in from the board's right as it opens, in the same quick motion, the board narrowing alongside it, and slides back out to the right as it closes, the board widening as it goes; replacing what it holds with another story, drafting, or research changes its content in place, with no slide. Its content, and focus in it, are there as soon as it starts to open.
Every motion here takes about 150 milliseconds, never longer, and a move made while another is still under way starts from wherever the card is then, never queued behind it.

## Auto Start

Next sprint can start on its own: a "Start automatically" switch on Next sprint's heading, beside Send sprint, its tooltip saying the next sprint starts as soon as the current one is done. It starts off, and is saved with the plan, in `order.json`, so it is kept across reloads and restarts.
While it is on, once every story of Current sprint has ended Done, the current sprint closes by itself, as Close sprint closes it, and Next sprint, if it holds a story, is sent at once, as Send sprint sends it, with nobody having to start it; and while no sprint is current, a story added to an empty Next sprint starts it the same way. A sprint that ended with a story failed, cancelled, stopped, or with its task missing, never starts the next by itself: it waits, Close sprint offered as ever, and the switch's row says, in the theme's warning colour, why the next didn't start. Nor does the next start while planning is paused, as the paused section says: it starts once the pause is ended by Resume, or Approve, if the switch is still on. An empty Next sprint starts nothing.
Each time a sprint starts by itself, a passive notification says so, "Next sprint started: 4 stories", with a link that opens Planning, and the debug log records it. Turning the switch off never stops a sprint already sent; it only keeps the next from starting by itself. Turning it on while no sprint is current and Next sprint holds a story starts Next sprint at once, as adding a story to it would, unless planning is paused.
The switch works while Planning isn't open, from the plan as saved, whichever tab is shown. When the project is opened, or the application starts, with the switch on, no sprint current, and Next sprint holding a story, it doesn't start by itself; the switch's row says, muted, "Waiting to start", with a "Start now" button, so a sprint never begins unseen as the application opens. A current sprint whose stories were cut off when the application quit, as every run is, ended them, and never starts the next by itself.
While the switch is on, Next sprint's heading shows "Auto" beside its count, in the theme's accent, and the ribbon's Send Sprint button's tooltip says the next sprint starts automatically.

## Saving

The stories, their order, and which section each is in are saved with the project's data, as the [ProjectData](../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, in `.suspense/planning/`, a file per story, holding its hidden anchor as a queued prompt's is, and an `order.json` listing the sections and their stories, so the plan is kept with the project and comes back as it was left. A story's steps are saved in its own file, in their order, as its steps say, never apart from it.

## Steps

A story can have steps: one or more further prompts, each a piece of the story done after the one before, as a chain's steps are. Each step has a prompt, a mode of its own, Code or Spec, starting as the story's, and a model and effort, starting as the story's, and may have attachments. A story with no steps is just its own prompt, as before; its prompt is always its first step.
An open story lists its steps beneath its prompt, in order, each a row numbered from 2, the story's own prompt being 1, with its mode pill and the first line of its prompt, opening in place to edit, as a story does. "Add step", beneath the last, adds one at the end, open and focused; several can be added one after another, Enter in an empty step's prompt adding none. Steps are reordered by dragging, as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, or Alt+Up and Alt+Down, and each has a remove button in its row and in its menu. The story's own prompt stays first and can't be moved among them.
A step belongs to its story and to nothing else. It is saved in the story's file, in a `steps` list of the story's hidden anchor, in its order, and saved as every change to the plan is, straight away; a story duplicated copies its steps, and one deleted deletes them. Its order is kept wherever the story goes, between sections, into a sprint, and back from Done.
Wherever the story is shown, its steps are too: its card in Planning shows how many beneath its title, muted, as "3 steps", with the list in its tooltip; the open story lists them as above; a proposal to add to it shows them, so what it would add to can be seen; and once it is sent, it is sent as a chain, its prompt first and each step after it in order, each step sent only once the one before it finishes, as the [PromptEditor](../prompt-mode/index.md#prompt-editor)'s chained tasks are, so the Tasks tab shows the story as one chain with its steps beneath it. A story sent can't be given more steps; its steps, sent or still to come, read as they were sent. In Current sprint, a story with steps lists its steps on its card, beneath its title, a line for each step, in order, each with its number, the first line of its prompt cut off with an ellipsis, and its own status, as a running chain's are in the Tasks tab; in Done, and in a finding started from the story, its steps are listed the same way, collapsed to its step count until it is expanded. The same steps, in the same order, are what every place shows, since every place reads them from the story's own file.
A step is only ever added to a story that exists. Adding one to a story that doesn't, as one deleted while a proposal naming it waited, or by another window, or whose file was removed from `.suspense/planning/` meanwhile, changes nothing: no story is made for it, no other story is given it, and nothing is saved. It says so in plain words where it was asked for, as "That story no longer exists, so the step wasn't added", in the theme's error colour, as the states say, with what was to be added kept, so it can be added to another story or as a new one. A step added to a story already sent is refused the same way, saying the story has been sent.

## Layout

Everything in Planning is laid out on one rhythm, so the board scans at a glance. The board fills the body beneath the tab bar, with 24 pixels of padding at its top, sides, and foot. Its columns are all the same fixed width, 320 pixels, 16 pixels apart, each as tall as the board, set side by side from its left edge in the order work moves, Backlog, Next sprint, Current sprint, Done, and Findings, the last. Each column is a list, as Trello draws one: a container of its own, as the parts draw a list, on the theme's recessed surface, one step from the base the board is on, its corners rounded 8 pixels, with its heading and its cards inside it; its surface and the gaps between columns set it apart, and it has no border.
Each column's heading reads as Linear heads a group: a row 32 pixels tall at the list's top, holding, from its left, the column's status icon, 14 pixels, as the parts give it; its name in small semibold text, in the theme's primary text colour; its count beside it, muted; and its actions at its right, each a labelled button, never an icon alone, as the sections give them: "Draft stories" and "Research" on the Backlog; "Send sprint" and "Start automatically" on Next sprint; "Close sprint" on Current sprint, once its sprint can close. A heading with more actions than fit its width wraps them onto a second line beneath its name rather than cutting any off. On the Backlog and Next sprint, hovering the heading, or focus anywhere in it, shows "+ Add" just after its count, a small ghost button with a plus icon and its label, never the icon alone, its tooltip saying it adds a story at the top of the list; it takes its room in the heading whether shown or not, so the heading's actions never shift as it appears, and the other columns' headings have none. 8 pixels beneath the heading come its cards, one beneath another, 8 pixels apart, each the list's full inner width.
At the foot of the Backlog and of Next sprint, 8 pixels beneath its last card, or beneath its empty state, is its "Add story" line: a row 32 pixels tall, the list's full inner width, with a plus icon and the label "Add story" in small muted text, its corners rounded 6 pixels, and no border; hovered, it takes the theme's hover surface and its text the theme's primary text colour. It scrolls with the cards, after the last of them. Its composer, as creating says, is drawn where it was clicked, at the foot in the line's place, or at the top, above the first card, from "+ Add": a story card, as the parts draw one, its title a text box in the card's title text, with the focus ring around the card, and beneath it, muted, "Enter to add, Escape to cancel"; the cards below it move down to make room, and the list scrolls to keep it in view. Current sprint, Done, and Findings have no "Add story" line.
Each column scrolls up and down on its own, its heading staying at its top while its cards scroll beneath it, inside the list's rounded corners, with the [Scrollbar](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar) shown along the list's right, inside it, while it holds more than fits. The board scrolls sideways when its columns are wider than the tab, with the [Scrollbar](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar) along its foot; while they fit, it doesn't scroll. Every card's state reads the same way, as below, and every label is the same small text, muted where it is secondary.
The side panel is the one place anything opens: an open story, Draft stories, and Research, never beneath a heading or a card, and never in a popup or over the board. A composer is not an opened story but a card being written, and is the one thing drawn in a list, where its story will sit. It is docked at the right of Planning's tab, 400 pixels wide, as tall as the tab, from the tab bar down to the chat input, a 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour along its left edge, and it scrolls up and down on its own, its heading staying at its top, with the [Scrollbar](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar) along its right while it holds more than fits. Only one thing is in it at a time: opening a story, drafting, or research replaces whatever it held, and closing it leaves nothing there. While it is open the board narrows to the space left of it, its columns keeping their width and scrolling sideways as ever when they no longer fit; the panel never covers the board, and the board never covers it. Closed, it takes no space and the board fills the tab again. It slides in and out at the right, as motion says.
While paused, the pause bar runs across the top of the whole board, above every column, as the paused section says, beside the side panel when it is open, never over it. Each column is headed as above, so nothing sits outside the rhythm, and an open story, a drafting or research panel, and the citations and steps inside a story all use the same five parts, below.

## Parts

Everything in Planning is built from five parts, each always drawn the same way, in the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode:
- A list: one per column, as the layout places it, 320 pixels wide and as tall as the board, on the theme's recessed surface, one step from the base, with no border, its corners rounded 8 pixels, 8 pixels of padding; its heading row at its top, as the layout says, then its cards, or its empty state centred beneath its heading; its heading's status icon one per column, each always the same: the Backlog a dashed circle in the theme's tertiary text colour; Next sprint an empty circle in the theme's secondary text colour; Current sprint a half-filled circle in the theme's accent; Done a filled circle with a check in the theme's success colour; and Findings a magnifying glass in the theme's secondary text colour; each only repeating the column's name, never standing for it

85	## Layout
86	
87	Everything in Planning is laid out on one rhythm, so the board scans at a glance. The board fills the body beneath the tab bar, with 24 pixels of padding at its top, sides, and foot. Its columns are all the same fixed width, 320 pixels, 16 pixels apart, each as tall as the board, set side by side from its left edge in the order work moves, Backlog, Next sprint, Current sprint, Done, and Findings, the last. Each column is a list, as Trello draws one: a container of its own, as the parts draw a list, on the theme's recessed surface, one step from the base the board is on, its corners rounded 8 pixels, with its heading and its cards inside it; its surface and the gaps between columns set it apart, and it has no border.
88	Each column's heading reads as Linear heads a group: a row 32 pixels tall at the list's top, holding, from its left, the column's status icon, 14 pixels, as the parts give it; its name in small semibold text, in the theme's primary text colour; its count beside it, muted; and its actions at its right, each a labelled button, never an icon alone, as the sections give them: "Draft stories" and "Research" on the Backlog; "Send sprint" and "Start automatically" on Next sprint; "Close sprint" on Current sprint, once its sprint can close. A heading with more actions than fit its width wraps them onto a second line beneath its name rather than cutting any off. On the Backlog and Next sprint, hovering the heading, or focus anywhere in it, shows "+ Add" just after its count, a small ghost button with a plus icon and its label, never the icon alone, its tooltip saying it adds a story at the top of the list; it takes its room in the heading whether shown or not, so the heading's actions never shift as it appears, and the other columns' headings have none. 8 pixels beneath the heading come its cards, one beneath another, 8 pixels apart, each the list's full inner width.
89	At the foot of the Backlog and of Next sprint, 8 pixels beneath its last card, or beneath its empty state, is its "Add story" line: a row 32 pixels tall, the list's full inner width, with a plus icon and the label "Add story" in small muted text, its corners rounded 6 pixels, and no border; hovered, it takes the theme's hover surface and its text the theme's primary text colour. It scrolls with the cards, after the last of them. Its composer, as creating says, is drawn where it was clicked, at the foot in the line's place, or at the top, above the first card, from "+ Add": a story card, as the parts draw one, its title a text box in the card's title text, with the focus ring around the card, and beneath it, muted, "Enter to add, Escape to cancel"; the cards below it move down to make room, and the list scrolls to keep it in view. Current sprint, Done, and Findings have no "Add story" line.
90	Each column scrolls up and down on its own, its heading staying at its top while its cards scroll beneath it, inside the list's rounded corners, with the [Scrollbar](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar) shown along the list's right, inside it, while it holds more than fits. The board scrolls sideways when its columns are wider than the tab, with the [Scrollbar](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar) along its foot; while they fit, it doesn't scroll. Every card's state reads the same way, as below, and every label is the same small text, muted where it is secondary.
91	The side panel is the one place anything opens: an open story, Draft stories, and Research, never beneath a heading or a card, and never in a popup or over the board. A composer is not an opened story but a card being written, and is the one thing drawn in a list, where its story will sit. It is docked at the right of Planning's tab, 400 pixels wide, as tall as the tab, from the tab bar down to the chat input, a 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour along its left edge, and it scrolls up and down on its own, its heading staying at its top, with the [Scrollbar](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar) along its right while it holds more than fits. Only one thing is in it at a time: opening a story, drafting, or research replaces whatever it held, and closing it leaves nothing there. While it is open the board narrows to the space left of it, its columns keeping their width and scrolling sideways as ever when they no longer fit; the panel never covers the board, and the board never covers it. Closed, it takes no space and the board fills the tab again. It slides in and out at the right, as motion says.
92	While paused, the pause bar runs across the top of the whole board, above every column, as the paused section says, beside the side panel when it is open, never over it. Each column is headed as above, so nothing sits outside the rhythm, and an open story, a drafting or research panel, and the citations and steps inside a story all use the same five parts, below.
93	
94	## Parts
95	
96	Everything in Planning is built from five parts, each always drawn the same way, in the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode:
97	- A list: one per column, as the layout places it, 320 pixels wide and as tall as the board, on the theme's recessed surface, one step from the base, with no border, its corners rounded 8 pixels, 8 pixels of padding; its heading row at its top, as the layout says, then its cards, or its empty state centred beneath its heading; its heading's status icon one per column, each always the same: the Backlog a dashed circle in the theme's tertiary text colour; Next sprint an empty circle in the theme's secondary text colour; Current sprint a half-filled circle in the theme's accent; Done a filled circle with a check in the theme's success colour; and Findings a magnifying glass in the theme's secondary text colour; each only repeating the column's name, never standing for it
98	- A story card: a box the full inner width of its list, on the theme's raised surface, with a 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour, corners rounded 6 pixels, 8 pixels of padding above and below and 10 at its sides, 8 pixels from the next; a top line with its drag grip, 16 pixels, in the theme's tertiary text colour, at its left, its title beside it, the card's primary text, in up to two lines, cut off with an ellipsis after the second, and its menu button at its right on hover and always while it is focused; beneath the title, 4 pixels below it, a single property row, 20 pixels tall, in small muted text, of small items 8 pixels apart: its mode pill, in its mode's colour, as the PromptModes colours it, its step count, its attachment icon, each when it has them, and its status and time, right-aligned, once it has been sent; and, in Current sprint, its steps' lines beneath, as its steps say; used for every story, in every column, muted in Done. Its states are three distinct steps, as the Theme's hierarchy orders them: hovering raises it one surface step, to the theme's hover surface; the open story keeps a 3 pixel line in the theme's accent along its left edge, as the stories say, whether or not it is hovered; and focus shows the theme's focus ring, in the accent, 2 pixels around it, over either, so a hover is always quieter than the open story's line, and that line quieter than focus
99	- A row: 36 pixels tall, for steps in an open story and for findings; its secondary text muted and cut off with an ellipsis, its buttons small ghost buttons with labels, shown at its right on hover and always while it is focused
100	- A panel: the side panel, docked at the board's right, full height, as the layout places it, on the theme's raised surface, its corners square, 12 pixels of padding, a heading row of 32 pixels with its name, as "Draft stories", "Research", or the story's title, and its close button, its content beneath, and its actions in a footer row, right-aligned, the primary action last; used for an open story, drafting, and research
101	- A card: a box inside a panel, on the theme's base surface, with a 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour, corners rounded 4 pixels, 12 pixels of padding, 8 pixels from the next; a label row at its top, its content, and a footer row of labelled buttons; used for proposals and for each finding's summary
102	Labels are words, never icons alone: every button reads what it does, "Accept", "Send sprint", "Start automatically", and an icon beside a label only repeats it. Each heading's count is a plain number, muted, and each status a coloured label, as the states say. The pause bar is a row across the whole board's top, above its columns, 40 pixels tall, its text and buttons on one line, the same height whatever it says.
103	
104	## States
105	
106	Each part of Planning has the same few states, shown the same way wherever they come up, so a state is never guessed from what is missing.
107	- Empty: a single muted line, centred in the column beneath its heading, saying what is missing and what to do, as "Nothing planned. Drag stories here, or press Ctrl+N.", with no illustration
108	- Loading: a spinner and a short muted label of what is happening, as "Drafting stories…", in the place the result will appear, never a blank space
109	- Paused: a story whose task is paused shows "Paused" as its status, in the theme's warning colour, with a small pause icon, and a "Resume" button on its card, as the PromptSending says of pausing; a sprint with any story paused says so in its heading, as "1 paused", in the same colour
110	- Error: a line in the theme's error colour, saying what went wrong in plain words, with what the harness or the application reported beneath it collapsed under "Details", and a "Try again" button where trying again can help
111	A story's status on its card is the same coloured label a task has, as the [MessageList](../prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#message-list)'s status says, Queued, Running with its spinner and time, Done, Failed, Cancelled, Paused, or, where its task can't be found, Task missing, as the sprint says, and a story not yet sent shows nothing there, so its absence means "not sent".
112	Each part shows each state that can come up for it, worded for it:
113	- Story list: empty, "Nothing planned. Press Ctrl+N to add a story." in Next sprint, "Nothing waiting." in the Backlog, "No sprint under way. Send sprint to start one." in Current sprint, and "Nothing done yet." in Done; loading, while the plan is read on opening, a few skeleton cards in each column, never an empty column; error, when the plan can't be read or saved, saying which file and why, with "Try again"
114	- Research and its findings: loading, the live line of what it is reading with its spinner; empty, "No findings yet." in Findings; error, the run's failure with "Try again", which keeps the question in its box; a finding that ended early, as stopped, marked "Incomplete", muted, in its row
115	- Pause: the pause bar, in the theme's warning colour, as the paused section says, and the sprint's Send buttons disabled with their tooltips saying why; a sprint that can't start for a failed story says so in its heading, in the same colour
116	- Proposals: loading, the drafting line and spinner; empty, "No stories proposed." with "Draft again"; error, the run's failure with "Try again"; a proposal with no spec cited, in the warning colour with "Draft again", as the spec grounding says
117	
118	----
119	## Keyboard
120	
121	Everything in Planning can be done from the keyboard. Tab moves through the columns' heading buttons, "+ Add" among them on the Backlog and Next sprint, the cards and rows, each list's "Add story" line after its last card, and the open story's fields in order, and the focused one shows the theme's focus ring. In a column, Up and Down move between its cards and rows, Down from the last reaching its "Add story" line, where Enter opens the composer, and Left and Right move focus to the column beside it, onto its card or row nearest the focused one's height, skipping a column with none, and scrolling the board sideways to show it; Enter opens or closes the focused story, A accepts the focused proposal, E edits it, and R rejects it. Alt+Up and Alt+Down move the focused story up or down within its column, and Alt+Left and Alt+Right move it into the column beside it, as dragging does, where that column takes it: from the Backlog Alt+Right moves it to the end of Next sprint, and from Next sprint Alt+Left moves it to the end of the Backlog, focus going with it; anywhere else, as a story in Current sprint or Done, or toward a column that takes no drops, they do nothing. Ctrl+N (Cmd+N on macOS) opens the composer at the foot of the list that has focus, the Backlog or Next sprint, when focus is on its heading, one of its cards, or its "Add story" line, and at the foot of Next sprint otherwise, as when focus is in Current sprint, Done, Findings, the side panel, or nowhere on the board, scrolling the board sideways to show it. In a composer, Enter adds the story and opens the next composer beneath it, focus moving to its title, and Escape discards it, focus going back to what opened it, the "Add story" line or the heading's "+ Add". Ctrl+Enter moves the focused story to Next sprint, or to the Backlog from it, Ctrl+Shift+Enter sends the sprint, and M opens the focused story's mode picker, whose options are picked with the arrow keys and Enter. Delete deletes the focused story after a confirmation. Escape closes what is open, a composer, a menu, then the side panel, whether it holds a story, drafting, or research, one at a time. Every button and control has a label a screen reader reads, as its visible text or, for an icon, its tooltip, and each shortcut is given in the tooltip of the control it stands for.
122	Ctrl+Shift+D opens Draft stories, focusing its request box, where Enter starts the draft, as Ctrl+Enter also does, and Shift+Enter adds a new line; Ctrl+Shift+R opens Research, focusing its box, where Ctrl+Enter starts it; F6 moves focus between the board's regions, the pause bar, each column, the side panel when it is open, and back, so each is a single stop; within the pause bar, Tab reaches Resume and Approve and send sprint; within an open story, Tab reaches its steps, its Add step, and its Spec citations, each citation opening on Enter; and within Findings, Enter opens the focused finding in its tab. The Start automatically switch is reached by Tab on Next sprint's heading and toggled with Space. Focus never lands on something hidden or disabled, and after an action it stays where it was or moves to what the action made, as the new story or the next proposal, never back to the top.
